title: Functional trait dissimilarity drives arboreal ant community assembly while competitive trait hierarchies shape colony performance in experimental mesocosms
content:
Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.


Abstract

Many broad-scale studies along spatial and habitat gradients show that organisms' traits can strongly influence community assembly by facilitating dispersal and environmental filtering. Nonetheless, how traits structure local faunal communities within habitats remains poorly understood. In particular, the often-assumed role of traits in affecting the outcome of competition among animal species is rarely tested. We coupled a field study with a mesocosm experiment to explore how arboreal ant species' traits shaped competition and community structure, leveraging a small mangrove ecosystem which conceivably imposed minimal dispersal and environmental filtering effects on ant community assembly. We first surveyed the ant communities inhabiting 115 mangrove trees using >2000 carbohydrate and protein baits, and measured multiple morphological, physiological (critical thermal maximum) and dietary (stable isotope trophic position) traits of all ant species. We then coupled co-occurrence network analyses with meta-analytical models to uncover the trait-based mechanisms structuring species co-occurrences in the field. Finally, in a mesocosm experiment, we reared 87 colonies of eight ant species from the mangrove over 30 days under different competition treatments to investigate trait-mediated effects of competition on ant colony performance. Patterns of ant species co-occurrences and bait recruitment indicated strong competition for limited protein-rich resources. Accordingly, dissimilarities in three traits—eye size, pronotum width and antennal scape length—consistently explained species co-occurrences, suggesting that the communities were competitively assembled by a partitioning of resource acquisition strategies among species. Species co-occurrences were also, to a lesser extent, explained by similarities in critical thermal limits, suggesting mild environmental filtering. In the mesocosm experiment, increasing directional differences in eye size and pronotum width between neighbouring ant colonies exacerbated interspecific competitive effects on colony survival and growth. Our results empirically demonstrate that traits linked to resource acquisition shape both coexistence and exclusion in ants. More broadly, by contrasting field patterns of niche partitioning with experimentally measured competitive effects, we show that the same traits can underpin stabilising processes that promote coexistence through limiting similarity, or equalising processes that drive exclusion through hierarchical differences, with their relative importance shifting across spatial scales and environmental contexts.

摘要

許多橫跨空間與棲地梯度的研究指出，生物性狀能促進擴散與環境篩選，在群落構建中扮演關鍵角色。然而，在單一棲地內，性狀如何影響動物群落結構與物種間競爭，仍缺乏實證檢驗。 本研究結合野外調查與中型生態箱實驗，探討樹棲螞蟻的性狀如何塑造競爭關係與群落構建。研究在一個細小的紅樹林進行，以降低擴散與環境篩選對螞蟻群落構建的影響。 我們於 115 棵紅樹上設置超過 2000 個碳水化合物與蛋白質誘餌，以調查螞蟻群落。我們亦測量螞蟻的形態性狀、生理性狀(臨界耐熱溫度)及飲食性狀(穩定同位素營養位階)。透過物種共現網絡與統合分析，我們檢視性狀與物種共現的關係；此外，在中型生態箱實驗中，我們飼養 8 種螞蟻共 87 個巢群，歷時一個月以上，以評估其性狀在不同競爭情境下對巢群存活與生長的影響。 野外調查顯示，螞蟻對有限的高蛋白質資源存在強烈競爭。物種在眼睛大小、前胸背板寬度與觸角柄長度上的差異能解釋其共現關係，反映群落構建是由資源獲取策略的差異所促進。另外，臨界耐熱溫度的相似性在較小程度上解釋物種共現，反映環境篩選作用。 中型生態箱實驗進一步證實，眼睛大小與前胸背板寬度上的差異能加劇跨物種競爭，對巢群的存活與生長不利。 本研究提供實證證據，顯示與獲取資源相關的性狀能同時促進物種共存與排除。我們亦指出，同一性狀既可透過極限相似性促進穩定化機制，使物種共存；亦可透過性狀差異促進均等化機制，導致物種互相排除。兩者的重要性會隨空間尺度與環境脈絡而變化。
